questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.title: == vs .equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`==`** compares **references** (memory addresses) for objects and raw **values** for primitives, while **`.equals()`** compares the **logical content** of objects. For Strings, `==` can deceptively return `true` because identical literals share one object in the **String pool**, so always use `.equals()` for content comparison.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands reference vs value comparison and knows that == on Strings is unreliable because of String pool sharing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare String content and getting false negatives on data from forms, files, or databases, or assuming == always compares values
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that string literals share references in the pool, making == accidentally pass in tests but fail in production — and use the null-safe "literal".equals(var) pattern

sections.title: == Is an Address Check; .equals() Is a Content Check
sections.content:
In Java you often need to check whether two things are the same, and Java gives you two ways to do it — the `==` operator and the `.equals()` method. They look like they do the same job, but they ask different questions.

Why have two? Because "the same" can mean two different things. It can mean "these are literally the same object," or it can mean "these hold the same content." Java keeps those ideas apart, and picking the wrong one is where bugs come from.

Here is how each works. Every variable in Java is a small box, called a **slot**. For **primitive** types like `int` or `boolean`, the slot holds the actual value, so `==` compares real values: `5 == 5` is always `true`. For **object** types like `String`, the slot does not hold the object itself — it holds a **reference**, which is the memory address where the object lives. So `==` on objects asks "do both boxes hold the same address?", not "is the content the same?" Think of two printed copies of one book: `==` asks if they are the same physical copy, while `.equals()` asks if the text inside matches.

The `.equals()` method compares **content**. `String` is written to compare character by character, so it answers the question you usually care about.

The nuance interviewers look for is the **String pool**. When you write the same text as a literal twice — `String a = "hi"` and `String b = "hi"` — Java stores it once and points both variables at it, so `a == b` returns `true`. That makes `==` look safe for strings.

The gotcha: the moment a string comes from user input, a file, a database, or `new String("hi")`, it is a fresh object with a different address. Now `==` returns `false` even though the characters match — a check that passes in tests but fails in production.

sections.title: How Java Decides Which Comparison Applies
sections.content:
Walk through any comparison by asking two questions: is this a primitive or an object, and if it is an object, did someone override equals? The diagram shows the decision path. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["You write a == b"] --> B{"Is it a primitive?
int, double, boolean.."} B -- Yes --> C["Compare actual values
5 == 5 → true"] B -- No --> D["Compare memory addresses
(same object on heap?)"] D --> E{"Are both pointing
to the String pool?"} E -- Yes --> F["== returns true
(accidental pool sharing)"] E -- No --> G["== returns false
even if content matches"] H["You write a.equals(b)"] --> I{"Is equals()
overridden?"} I -- Yes --> J["Compare logical content
String: char by char"] I -- No --> K["Falls back to ==
same as reference check"] ``` Notice that pool sharing makes `==` accidentally return `true` for identical string literals — which is why relying on it is dangerous. Always use `.equals()` for String content.

sections.title: Wrong — == on a String that came from runtime
Right — .equals() compares content (null-safe form)
When to Reach for == and When for .equals()
sections.content:
The decision is mechanical once you know the rule, and getting it right is half of what the interviewer is checking.

Use `==` when you are comparing **primitives** (`int`, `char`, `boolean`, `double`) — there the slot holds the actual value, so `==` genuinely compares values. Also use `==` for **`null` checks** (`if (obj == null)`) and for **enum** constants, because each enum value is a single shared instance, so reference equality is exactly what you want — `status == Status.ACTIVE` is both correct and idiomatic.

Use `.equals()` for **everything else**: any time you are asking "do these two objects hold the same content?" That covers `String`, `Integer`, `BigDecimal`, `LocalDate`, and your own classes once you override `equals()`. If you are comparing the text inside two strings, `.equals()` is the only correct tool — `==` will betray you the moment one side is not a literal.

A simple habit keeps you out of trouble: if the type has a meaningful "same value" idea, reach for `.equals()`; reserve `==` for primitives, null, and enums.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Comparing String content with `==`** — it checks object identity, not text, so `inputName == "admin"` returns `false` for runtime input even when the characters match, silently breaking logins and lookups.
- **Being fooled by passing tests** — string literals share one object in the pool, so `"hi" == "hi"` is `true`; this makes `==` *look* correct in unit tests, then fail in production on database- or form-sourced strings.
- **Calling `.equals()` on a possibly-null reference** — `userInput.equals("admin")` throws `NullPointerException` when `userInput` is null; flip it to `"admin".equals(userInput)` so a null returns `false` instead.
- **Overriding `equals()` but not `hashCode()`** — your custom class then "works" in an `if`, but behaves incorrectly inside a `HashMap` or `HashSet`, where lookups silently miss.

sections.title: == vs .equals() at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|== operator|~Compares the variable's slot|primitives: actual value|objects: memory address|fast, but not content
blue|.equals()|~Compares logical content|Object default = ==|override for value equality|String/Integer override it
emerald|String pool|~Literals share one object|"hi" == "hi" is true|new String("hi") is false|why == feels like it works
rose|Safe habit|~Use .equals() for content|null-safe: "x".equals(v)|== only for primitives/enums|enums are singletons

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`==` on primitives** — compares actual values (`5 == 5` is `true`).
- **`==` on objects** — compares memory addresses, not content.
- **String pool** — identical literals share one object, so `==` can deceptively pass in tests but fail in production.
- **`.equals()`** — compares logical content; override it in custom classes.
- **Null-safe habit** — write `"literal".equals(var)` to dodge `NullPointerException`.
- **Use `==` for enums** — they are singletons, so reference equality is correct.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The thing to get straight is **what each one actually compares**. `==` checks whether two variables point to the **same object in memory**; `.equals()` checks whether they hold the **same content**.

For strings that distinction bites people, and the reason is the **String pool**. Two identical literals like `"hello"` share one pooled object, so `==` returns `true` — which is exactly why it slips through unit tests. But the moment a string comes from a form or a database, it's a fresh object, and `==` returns `false` even though the text is identical. That's a login check that **passes in tests and quietly fails in production**.

So for any content comparison I use `.equals()`, and I put the literal on the left — `"admin".equals(username)` — so a `null` value returns `false` instead of throwing. I reserve `==` for **primitives, null checks, and enums**, where reference comparison is genuinely what I want.

questions.question: What is the difference between pre-increment (++i) and post-increment (i++) in Java?
questions.title: Pre-increment vs Post-increment in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Pre-increment `++i`** adds 1 first and then returns the **new** value; **post-increment `i++`** returns the **current** value first and then adds 1. The difference only shows up when the expression's value is used in an assignment or calculation — as standalone statements they are identical.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of expression evaluation order and operator side effects, usually probed with tricky output-prediction questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ++i and i++ always differ, or expecting int b = i++ to give b the incremented value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a compound expression like int b = ++i + i++ step by step, showing what each operator returns and when i changes

sections.title: It Is All About Timing: When Does the Increment Happen?
sections.content:
In Java, both `i++` and `++i` are ways to add 1 to a variable. You will see them constantly — counting in loops, stepping through arrays — so it is worth knowing exactly how they differ.

Why are there two forms at all? Because adding 1 is sometimes only half of what you want. Often you also want to *use* the variable's value on the same line — and the two forms let you choose whether you use the value before the 1 is added or after.

Here is how each works. Both forms always add 1 to the variable. The difference is **which value gets handed to the rest of the line**. `++i` is "prepare then present": it adds 1 first, then gives back the new value. `i++` is "present then prepare": it gives back the current value first, then adds 1. Picture a cash register that prints a receipt number and then advances its counter — pre-increment advances first and prints the new number, post-increment prints the current number and advances afterward.

The nuance interviewers check: **when the value is not used, there is no difference at all**. A line like `i++;` on its own, or the update part of a `for` loop, adds 1 either way — nothing reads what comes back. The two forms only diverge when you capture the value, like `int b = i++;`.

The gotcha lives there. With `i = 5`, `int b = i++` gives `b` the value `5` — the *old* value — and then `i` becomes `6`; most people expect `b` to be `6`. Switch to `int b = ++i` and `b` is `6`. Interviewers push further with `int b = ++i + i++` starting at `i = 5`: Java goes left to right, so `++i` makes `i` `6` and contributes `6`, then `i++` contributes `6` and makes `i` `7`, giving `b = 12` and `i = 7`. Tracing that calmly is what sets you apart.

sections.title: The Two-Step Order That Decides the Value
sections.content:
Both operators do the same two things — return a value and add 1 — but in opposite order. Tracing that order with `i = 5` makes every output-prediction question fall out automatically.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Expression uses i (i = 5)"] --> B{"Which operator?"}
    B -- "++i (pre)" --> C["Step 1: i becomes 6"]
    C --> D["Step 2: hand 6 to the expression"]
    B -- "i++ (post)" --> E["Step 1: hand 5 to the expression"]
    E --> F["Step 2: i becomes 6"]
    D --> G["int b = ++i  →  b = 6, i = 6"]
    F --> H["int b = i++  →  b = 5, i = 6"]
```

The variable `i` lands on `6` either way — only the value handed to the expression differs. That single fork is the whole concept, and it is why the difference vanishes when nobody captures the returned value.

sections.title: Wrong assumption — post-increment returns the old value
sections.content:
Most freshers read `int b = i++` as "increment `i`, then store it in `b`" and expect `b` to be `6`. The operator actually hands over the value first and increments second.

```java
int i = 5;
int b = i++;            // fresher expects b == 6
System.out.println(b);  // 5 — post-increment returns the OLD value first
System.out.println(i);  // 6 — i was incremented afterwards
```

So `b` captures `5`, the value `i` had *before* the increment, while `i` itself moves on to `6`. The increment did happen — it just happened after the value was already taken.

sections.title: Right — pre-increment returns the new value
sections.content:
Switch to `++i` and the order flips: the increment runs first, so the value handed to `b` is already the new one.

```java
int i = 5;
int b = ++i;            // increment first, then return
System.out.println(b);  // 6 — new value is returned
System.out.println(i);  // 6
```

For the classic compound trap with `i = 5`: `int b = ++i + i++` — Java evaluates left to right, so `++i` makes `i = 6` and yields `6`; `i++` yields the current `6` and makes `i = 7`; the sum is `6 + 6`, giving `b = 12` and `i = 7`. Being able to trace that step by step is exactly what the interviewer is probing.

sections.title: Does the Choice Even Matter Here?
sections.content:
The practical question is not "which is faster" — for an `int`, the compiler produces identical bytecode and there is no performance difference. The real decision is whether the **returned value is being used at all**.

When the increment stands alone — a statement on its own line like `i++;`, or the update clause of a `for` loop like `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)` — the choice is irrelevant. Nothing reads the value, so `i++` and `++i` are interchangeable; pick whichever reads naturally. Most Java code uses `i++` in loops purely out of convention.

The choice **only** matters when you capture the result in the same expression — `int b = i++;`, `array[i++] = x;`, or `while (n-- > 0)`. There, post-increment lets you use the current value and advance the counter in one move, which is genuinely useful for array indexing and countdown loops.

The senior habit: outside of those tight idioms, do not chain `++` inside larger expressions. Clever one-liners that mix `++i` and `i++` are a readability cost with no upside — split them into clear statements.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting `int b = i++` to give the new value** — post-increment returns the *old* value first, so `b` gets `5` when `i` is `5`; `i` only becomes `6` afterwards.
- **Assuming `++i` and `i++` always differ** — as standalone statements (`i++;`) or in a `for` loop's update clause they are completely identical, because no one reads the returned value.
- **Chaining increments in one expression** — writing `int b = ++i + i++` is valid but a trap people misread; even when you get it right, it is a code-review red flag, so split it into separate statements.
- **Thinking pre-increment is faster for primitives** — for an `int` the JIT produces the same code; the C++ "prefer `++i`" advice about avoiding a temporary copy does not apply to Java primitives.

sections.title: ++i vs i++ at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|++i (pre)|~Increment, then read|i becomes i+1 first|returns the new value|prepare then present
blue|i++ (post)|~Read, then increment|returns the old value|i becomes i+1 after|present then prepare
emerald|Standalone|~Same effect|i++; equals ++i;|both add 1|no return value used
rose|In expressions|~Values differ|int b = ++i vs i++|array[i++] is common|avoid chaining ++ in one line

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`++i` (pre)** — increments first, then returns the new value.
- **`i++` (post)** — returns the current value, then increments.
- **Standalone usage** — `++i` and `i++` are identical when used alone on a line.
- **In expressions** — the difference only matters when the return value is captured.
- **For-loops** — `i++` is the convention, but `++i` works identically.
- **Readability** — avoid multiple increments in one expression; clarity beats cleverness.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Both operators add one to the variable — the only difference is **the order the value comes back**. **Pre-increment**, `++i`, increments first and then hands you the new value. **Post-increment**, `i++`, hands you the current value first and increments afterward.

So if `i` is 5 and I write `int b = i++`, `b` gets 5 and `i` becomes 6 — not the 6 most people expect. Switch to `++i` and `b` is 6. What candidates miss is that in a standalone statement, or in a for-loop's update clause, the two are **identical**, because nothing reads the returned value.

The difference only shows up when you capture it. The classic trap, `int b = ++i + i++` with `i` at 5, gives `b` twelve and `i` seven. In real code I keep these out of larger expressions — **clarity beats cleverness**.

questions.question: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java and how do && and || use it?
questions.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation with && and || in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Short-circuit evaluation** means Java stops evaluating a boolean expression as soon as the result is certain: with **`&&`**, a `false` left side skips the right; with **`||`**, a `true` left side skips the right. This is both a performance optimization and the standard **null-safety** pattern, e.g. `obj != null && obj.isValid()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows logical operators have execution-order implications beyond boolean logic, especially for null-safety guards
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming both sides of && or || always execute, leading to NullPointerExceptions or side effects that silently never run
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the null-safety pattern obj != null && obj.getName().equals("foo") and explain why order matters because evaluation is left-to-right

sections.title: Java Stops Early When It Already Knows the Answer
sections.content:
In Java you often need to check several yes/no conditions together in one `if`, and you join them with `&&` for AND or `||` for OR. There is something quietly important about how Java reads them.

Java reads these conditions from left to right and stops the instant the answer is certain. This is called **short-circuit evaluation**, and it exists so Java never does work it does not need to do. If the outcome is already decided by the left side, checking the right side is pointless.

Here is the mechanism, one piece at a time. With `&&` (AND), the whole expression is `false` the moment the left side is `false` — so the right side is skipped entirely. With `||` (OR), the whole expression is `true` the moment the left side is `true` — again the right side is skipped. Picture a checkpoint with two guards: if the first guard turns you away, the second guard never even sees you.

The nuance interviewers really want is **null safety**. Write `if (user != null && user.isActive())` and Java checks `user != null` first. If `user` is null, the left side is `false`, `&&` short-circuits, and `user.isActive()` is never called — so there is no `NullPointerException`. The null check acts as a gate guarding the method call to its right.

The gotcha is that **order is everything**. Flip it to `user.isActive() && user != null` and you crash immediately on a null user, because the method runs before the check. Two more traps: a side effect on the right, like a `counter++`, silently never runs when the left short-circuits; and `&` and `|` are *not* the same — they always evaluate both sides (they are really for bit-level work on integers), so using `&` in a null guard brings the crash right back.

sections.title: Short-Circuit Decision Path for && and ||
sections.content:
Tracing through how each operator decides whether to look at the right side makes the safety property obvious. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Evaluate left side"] --> B{"Operator type?"} B -- "&&" --> C{"Left is false?"} C -- Yes --> D["STOP — return false
Right side never runs"] C -- No --> E["Evaluate right side
Return right result"] B -- "||" --> F{"Left is true?"} F -- Yes --> G["STOP — return true
Right side never runs"] F -- No --> H["Evaluate right side
Return right result"] ``` Notice that `&&` short-circuits on `false` and `||` short-circuits on `true` — exactly the case where each already knows the answer. This is why the null check in `obj != null && obj.method()` must come first: if it returns false, the method call on the right is never reached.

sections.title: Wrong — null check placed after the method call
Right — null check first lets && short-circuit safely
When to Use && and || — and When & or | Instead
sections.content:
For boolean conditions, `&&` and `||` are almost always the right choice. They short-circuit, which means they double as a safety mechanism: the left side can guard the right, so you can null-check, range-check, or cache-check before doing anything expensive or risky. Order them cheapest-and-safest first — `cache.contains(key) || database.has(key)` only hits the database on a cache miss.

The non-short-circuiting `&` and `|` exist for two distinct jobs. Their main job is **bitwise arithmetic on integers** — `flags & MASK`, `permissions | WRITE` — manipulating individual bits, which has nothing to do with boolean logic. They also work on booleans, where they force **both** sides to evaluate.

That full evaluation is occasionally wanted: if the right side has a side effect you *need* to run regardless — say `valid = validateName(form) & validateEmail(form)` where each method must record its own error so the user sees every problem at once — `&` is the deliberate choice. But that is rare. For everyday conditions, reach for `&&` and `||`; using `&` on booleans is far more often a typo than an intention.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting the null check after the method call** — `user.length() > 0 && user != null` throws `NullPointerException` because the left side runs first; the guard must come before what it protects.
- **Relying on a side effect that gets skipped** — in `if (cheap() && counter++ > 0)`, when `cheap()` is `false` the `counter++` never runs; short-circuiting silently drops the right side, which can leave counters or logs out of sync.
- **Using `&` or `|` for boolean conditions** — `user != null & user.isActive()` compiles, but `&` evaluates both sides, so the null check no longer protects the method call and you get an NPE at runtime.
- **Assuming `||` is just `&&` reversed** — `&&` short-circuits on `false`, `||` short-circuits on `true`; mixing up which one stops early leads to the wrong branch running or expensive work happening when it should not.

sections.title: Short-Circuit Logic at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|AND (&&)|~Stops on false|false and anything is false|right side skipped|guards the right side
blue|OR (||)|~Stops on true|true or anything is true|right side skipped|early exit on success
emerald|Null safety|~Check before use|obj != null && obj.m()|order matters|null check always left
rose|Bitwise & and pipe|~No skipping|both sides always run|risk of NPE on booleans|meant for integers

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`&&`** — stops on a `false` left side; the right side never executes.
- **`||`** — stops on a `true` left side; the right side never executes.
- **Null safety pattern** — `obj != null && obj.method()` prevents `NullPointerException`.
- **Order matters** — Java evaluates strictly left-to-right, so guards go on the left.
- **Side effects may not run** — if the right side has a `counter++` or method call, it may be silently skipped.
- **`&` and `|`** — bitwise, always evaluate both sides — do not use them for boolean guards.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
**Short-circuit evaluation** means Java stops checking a logical expression the instant it knows the result. With `&&`, a `false` on the left makes the whole thing false, so the right side is skipped. With `||`, a `true` on the left does the same.

Why this matters more than performance is **null safety**. Writing `if (obj != null && obj.method())` works because when `obj` is `null` the left side is false, so Java never calls the method — the null check **guards everything to its right**. That makes **order critical**: put the cheap, safe check on the left.

The flip side is a trap — if you rely on a side effect on the right, like a `counter++`, it silently won't run when the left short-circuits. And `&` isn't a shortcut for `&&`; it always evaluates **both sides**, so using it here brings back the very null-pointer crash you were trying to avoid.

When would you intentionally use & instead of && ?

questions.question: What is the ternary operator in Java and how is it different from if-else?
questions.title: Ternary Operator in Java
questions.direct_answer: The **ternary operator** `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is Java's only three-operand operator and is an **expression** that produces a value, unlike `if-else` which is a **statement**. Because it returns a value, you can use it inline in assignments, method arguments, and return statements. Keep it to simple one-line binary choices — nest it and readability collapses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the expression-versus-statement distinction and when concise conditional syntax helps versus hurts readability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Nesting ternary operators deeply into unreadable code, or trying to use the ternary to execute actions rather than produce a value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the ternary is an expression you can drop inline, while if-else is a statement that executes blocks and can't be assigned

sections.title: The Ternary Operator Is a Compact Choice That Hands Back a Value
sections.content:
In Java, the **ternary operator** is a short way to pick between two values based on a condition. It is written `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`, and the name "ternary" simply means it has three parts.

Why does it exist? Because choosing one of two values is so common that a full `if-else` feels heavy for it. Normally you declare a variable, write an `if` that assigns one value, and an `else` that assigns another — four to six lines to make a single choice. The ternary does the same thing in one line: `String label = score >= 60 ? "Pass" : "Fail"`.

Here is the idea that makes it click, and the one interviewers probe. The ternary is an **expression**, not a **statement**. An expression *produces a value*; a statement *performs an action*. Because the ternary produces a value, you can put it anywhere a value is expected — the right side of an assignment, an argument inside a method call, or after a `return`. An `if-else` block cannot be dropped into those places, because it runs blocks rather than handing back a value. It even lets the variable be `final`, since the value is assigned in the same breath as the declaration.

The gotcha is overusing it. It shines for one simple choice on one line, like a default `name != null ? name : "Guest"`. But nest it — `a ? b ? c : d : e` — and it becomes almost unreadable. And it is built to *return* a value, not to *do* things; if a branch needs to call a method or update state for its side effect, that is `if-else`'s job. The moment it stops fitting cleanly on one line, switch back.

sections.title: One Condition, Two Possible Values, One Result
sections.content:
The ternary always does the same thing: evaluate the condition, then resolve to one of two values that flows straight into wherever you put it. Seeing it as a value-producer — not a mini if-else — is the mental model interviewers reward. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse"] --> B{"Is condition true?"} B -- Yes --> C["Expression resolves to valueIfTrue"] B -- No --> D["Expression resolves to valueIfFalse"] C --> E["That single value drops into the slot:
String g = ... ? a : b"] D --> E ``` Both branches converge on one value, and that value lands wherever the expression sits — an assignment, a method argument, or a return. An `if-else` cannot do that: it runs blocks, it does not hand back a value.

sections.title: Without ternary — verbose for a simple pick
With ternary — one expression, same result
Ternary or if-else? Pick by What You Need Back
sections.content:
Choose based on a single question: are you **producing a value** or **performing actions**?

Reach for the ternary when the answer is one of two values and the whole thing fits comfortably on one line. It shines for inline picks the language otherwise makes clumsy: a default fallback like `name != null ? name : "Guest"`, a value inside a method call such as `log.info(count == 1 ? "1 item" : count + " items")`, or a `return` that chooses between two results. In all of these, an `if-else` would force you to break the flow and introduce a temporary variable.

Reach for `if-else` the moment a branch needs to *do* something rather than *be* something — call a method, update several fields, throw an exception, log and continue. `if-else` is also the right call when the condition is complex or the expression no longer fits on one readable line.

The line I draw: if it does not read cleanly on one line, or any branch has a side effect, use `if-else`. Conciseness is only a win when it also improves clarity.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nesting ternaries deeply** — `a ? b ? c : d : e` is valid but nearly unreadable; one level is the practical limit, and anything beyond it belongs in `if-else` or a `switch`.
- **Using the ternary to run actions** — it is built to *produce a value*, not execute statements; if a branch needs to call a method or update state for its side effect, that is what `if-else` is for.
- **Type-mismatch surprises** — the two branches are coerced to a common type, so `flag ? 1 : 2.0` quietly promotes the `int` to `double`; mixed branch types can produce a value you did not expect.
- **Forgetting precedence in concatenation** — `"Score: " + n > 5 ? "high" : "low"` does not parse the way you think; wrap the ternary in parentheses: `"Score: " + (n > 5 ? "high" : "low")`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Syntax** — `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` returns one of two values.
- **Expression vs statement** — the ternary returns a value; `if-else` executes blocks.
- **Inline usage** — works in assignments, method calls, return statements, and string concatenation.
- **Readability rule** — simple one-line choices only; switch to `if-else` for complex logic.
- **Null-safe default pattern** — `name != null ? name : "Guest"` is the idiomatic fallback.
- **Nesting** — one level of nesting is borderline; deeper than that is a code review comment.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The cleanest framing is that the ternary is an **expression that produces a value**, while `if-else` is a **statement that runs blocks**. The syntax is `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

Because it hands back a value, you can drop it straight into an assignment, a method argument, or a return — `String status = isActive ? "online" : "offline"` does in one line what `if-else` needs four to do, and the variable can even be `final`. That **expression-versus-statement distinction** is what the interviewer is really testing.

It's ideal for **simple binary picks** and defaults, like `name != null ? name : "Guest"`. Where freshers go wrong is nesting ternaries until they're unreadable, or using one to run actions instead of return a value. My rule: **if it doesn't fit cleanly on one line, or a branch needs a side effect, use `if-else`**.

beats.text: The ternary is Java's one three-part operator. You write a condition, a value if true, and a value if false. It checks the condition. Then it returns one of the two values.
It's there for one thing — a clean choice between two values. A four-line if-else that only picks one value shrinks to a single line. The variable can even be `final`.

items: It's an expression, not a statement, so it produces a value that drops in inline.
An if-else is a statement. It runs blocks, so it can't sit inside another expression.
The non-obvious win. It lets the variable stay `final`, since the value lands in one step.

beats.text: Picture a Java app. A `final` label gets its value in one line. A condition picks the pass branch or the fail branch. An if-else block can't do that, since it assigns after the declaration. That's the point interviewers really want — expression versus statement.

items: Nesting ternaries more than one level deep, which turns the line unreadable.
Using one to run actions for a side effect. It's built to return a value, not to do things.
